strengths: Well-motivated practical contribution addressing real enterprise needs for deployable, privacy-preserving cybersecurity models with clear motivation around compliance and on-premises deployment

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation across 9 diverse cybersecurity benchmarks with proper methodology including zero-shot CoT evaluation, ablation studies, and LLM-as-Judge validation achieving >90% alignment with human experts
Strong empirical results showing 7-14% average improvements over baselines and competitive or superior performance on key threat intelligence benchmarks (CTI-RCM) compared to frontier models

Well-designed data enrichment pipeline with thoughtful expert-in-the-loop format definition system and multi-step evidence retrieval reducing hallucinations and improving data quality (85.62% readability preference, 9.25 factuality)
Good reproducibility practices with detailed training recipes, hyperparameters, hardware specifications, comprehensive appendices, and practical focus on quantization effects for deployment scenarios
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: primarily applies existing techniques (CoT reformatting, expert annotation, retrieval) to cybersecurity domain rather than proposing fundamentally new methods; ReAlign (Fan et al., 2024) is a very similar direct precursor

Evaluation limited to domain-specific closed-book benchmarks raising concerns about overfitting and generalization; no evaluation on out-of-domain tasks, realistic security workflows, or adversarial scenarios; benchmark format may favor models trained on similar data

Comparison fairness issues: specialized cybersecurity models compared to general-purpose models; no ablation where general models are fine-tuned on SecKnowledge 2.0; Sec-Gemini v1 is unreleased with sparse documentation

Dataset and training details underspecified: final SecKnowledge 2.0 size not explicitly stated, synthetic data generation process not fully detailed, only 2 epochs of training without convergence analysis, interesting base vs. post-trained finding (Table 3) under-explored with single model pair

Reproducibility limitations: relies on non-open base models (Qwen3, gpt-oss-20b), expert-in-the-loop pipeline difficult to reproduce exactly, web search produces variable results, no commitment to code/dataset release, gpt-oss-120b used for processing is not clearly identified

Incomplete ablations: no independent analysis of document grounding vs. web search, missing breakdown by cybersecurity domain, limited error analysis or failure case discussion, impact of 25% original data mixing not isolated

Generalization and scope concerns: narrow specialization to cybersecurity benchmarks with no assessment of general language understanding; no evaluation on realistic threat investigation workflows; evaluation on structured tasks only, not free-form analysis; no adversarial evaluation or red-teaming critical for security applications

Ethical and safety gaps: no discussion of potential misuse of security-specialized models, limited analysis of failure modes that could lead to incorrect security decisions, no red-teaming or adversarial robustness evaluation despite security context

Presentation issues: overclaimed statements (e.g., 'frontier cybersecurity performance' true only on specific benchmarks), reads as technical report rather than research contribution with general insights, core contributions could be clearer
Statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance testing, or convergence analysis reported despite making precise performance claims

strengths: Comprehensive evaluation across 9 diverse cybersecurity benchmarks with additional real-world use cases (threat report mapping, CVE reassessment, secure code generation)
Strong empirical results: 7-14% improvements over baselines, with 20B model ranking first on core threat-investigation tasks, outperforming GPT-4o, o1, o3-mini, and Sec-Gemini v1

Well-designed SecKnowledge 2.0 pipeline combining expert-in-the-loop format definition with LLM-guided multi-step grounding, achieving 85.62% preference for rewritten answers with 9.25 average factuality score
Rigorous ablation studies isolating contributions of data pipeline, search component, and backbone LLM, with clear demonstration that expert-defined formats provide substantial benefits
Interesting and well-supported finding that base models significantly outperform post-trained models for fine-tuning (15.16% vs 5.62% on key benchmarks), with empirical validation in Table 4
Addresses practical enterprise security needs: on-premises deployment, cost efficiency, compliance, with realistic training and inference requirements documented
Commitment to open-source release of models, pipeline, and evaluation benchmarks; extensive appendices enable reproducibility attempts
Validation of LLMaaJ results against human expert preferences showing 90%+ agreement with proper grounding, lending credibility to automated evaluation
Clear presentation with well-organized structure, concrete examples, and comprehensive implementation details
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily adapts existing data enrichment techniques (ReAlign from Fan et al. 2024) to cybersecurity domain with expert-in-the-loop modifications; no new training methods or architectures

Incremental contribution over prior work: SecKnowledge and evaluation suite established by same authors (Levi et al.); this work enhances the dataset and models rather than introducing fundamentally new approaches

Expert involvement not rigorously documented: no quantification of number of experts, their backgrounds, expertise verification, or inter-rater agreement on format definitions, limiting reproducibility
Lack of statistical significance testing: reported improvements lack confidence intervals or p-values; some gains are marginal and require statistical validation

Data quality assessment concerns: factuality scores appear optimistic (9.25/10 average); o3 used as judge without validation of potential biases; only 115 expert-written questions used for LLMaaJ validation
Frontier model evaluation incomplete: only evaluated on 2 benchmarks (CTIBench) to reduce cost; full suite evaluation would strengthen claims of parity with frontier models
Generalizability unclear: approach is tightly coupled to cybersecurity domain with domain-specific taxonomies; applicability to other specialized domains not explored

Potential data leakage concerns: SecKnowledge 2.0 partially rewrites SecKnowledge examples; overlap between training and evaluation benchmarks (both derived from security sources) not thoroughly analyzed
Evaluation limitations: test set sizes unknown for real-world use cases; CyberSOCEval malware analysis excluded due to context length; no error analysis or failure mode discussion
Reproducibility challenges: expert-in-the-loop format definition is inherently difficult to reproduce without identical expert panels; no metrics for measuring successful reproduction

strengths: Comprehensive evaluation across 9+ cybersecurity benchmarks with thorough ablation studies showing contribution of each pipeline component
Practical focus addressing real enterprise needs: on-premises deployment, privacy compliance, and cost efficiency for security operations
Detailed reproducibility documentation including training procedures, hyperparameters, inference latency, and quantization analysis
Plans for open-source release of models, pipeline code, and evaluation benchmarks to support community
Real-world use case validation beyond standard benchmarks (threat report mapping, CVE reassessment)
Solid experimental methodology with human validation of LLM-as-Judge (90% agreement with security experts)
weaknesses: Overclaimed results: Abstract claims 'ranks first' and 'frontier performance' but comparisons are unfair (specialized models trained on domain data vs general-purpose models not optimized for cybersecurity); Sec-Gemini v1 and o1 rank higher on CTI-MCQ
Limited novelty: Primarily combines existing techniques (expert-in-the-loop annotation, RAG, chain-of-thought, data reformatting from Fan et al. 2024) without algorithmic or theoretical contributions

Critical unresolved issue: Secure code generation shows 6.52% performance regression vs baselines (Table 17), dismissed as 'modest' without adequate explanation of why domain specialization harms this capability
Incomplete evaluation: CyberSOCEval malware analysis skipped entirely due to context window limitations (8k vs 128k required), undermining claims of practical deployment readiness

Unfair experimental design: Frontier models evaluated with simple zero-shot CoT prompting that may not be optimal; no ablation on prompting strategy; different models likely have different optimal settings

Expert-in-the-loop reproducibility barrier: Format definition process poorly quantified (rejection rates, iteration counts, actual labor required); training from base models vastly outperforms post-trained models (22.7% vs 1.85%) without adequate explanation
Hyperparameter choices unjustified: Learning rate, batch size, epochs, retrieval settings (K=2, R=2, limit to 4 results) lack principled justification beyond context window constraints
Unexplained technical anomaly: Base models learn 2.7× better than post-trained models despite claimed high data quality, suggesting unresolved training instability or data quality issues
Missing analysis: No error analysis, failure case discussion, or adversarial robustness evaluation; no comparison with vanilla RAG or other domain adaptation approaches
Dual-use safety concerns under-addressed: No red-teaming results; no evaluation on attack generation or evasion; promised 'responsible-use terms' lack specifics in main paper

strengths: Strong empirical results on cybersecurity benchmarks with competitive performance against frontier models (Sec-Gemini v1, o1, o3-mini, GPT-4o) on threat investigation tasks
Comprehensive evaluation across 9 diverse cybersecurity benchmarks with multiple evaluation methodologies (accuracy, LLM-as-Judge with 80-90% human agreement, real-world use cases)
Thorough ablation studies demonstrating contribution of each component (data pipeline +5.92%, search +3%, backbone LLM robustness)
Practical focus addressing enterprise constraints: on-premises deployment, privacy compliance, cost efficiency, secure coding evaluation

Reproducibility commitment with planned model/code release, detailed training specifications (learning rate, batch size, context length), inference latency analysis, and quality assessment pipeline (85.62% readability, 9.25 factuality score)
Systematic expert-in-the-loop data enrichment pipeline with quality validation and multi-step grounding to reduce hallucinations
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily applies existing techniques (ReAlign data enrichment, CoT reasoning, retrieval grounding) to cybersecurity domain rather than introducing new methods

Surprising finding about base models outperforming post-trained models (Table 4: 15.16% vs 5.62% improvement) only validated on single experiment (Qwen3-8B) and lacks theoretical explanation or broader investigation
Secure code generation regression (6.52% average degradation: 71.63% vs 79.47%) is downplayed despite material reduction in code safety for defensive automation scenarios

Evaluation limitations: LLM-as-Judge uses frontier model (o3) to evaluate against frontier models (circular); only 115 expert questions and 30 experts for human validation; 10% disagreement with/without grounding suggests judge unreliability

Incomplete frontier model comparison: detailed evaluation only on 2 benchmarks (CTI-MCQ, CTI-RCM); claims of 'outperforming' need clarification (ranks first on RCM only, second on MCQ); excluded malware analysis tasks due to context length limitations

Performance claims overstated in abstract/introduction: 'outperforms GPT-4o, o1, o3-mini, Sec-Gemini v1' is only true for one metric (CTI-RCM); mixed ranking across benchmarks warrants more precise framing
Retrieval grounding contribution modest (~3% average improvement, varies by benchmark) with arbitrary configuration choices (K=2, Rmax=8) insufficiently justified
Data contamination risks not addressed: SecEval is publicly available; many benchmarks use public sources that may overlap with training data
Incomplete real-world evaluation: CyberSOCEval malware analysis excluded (context window limitations), CVE reassessment shows modest gains (0.834 vs baseline 0.738-0.825)
